question: What are Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft each currently guiding for capital expenditures, and how do they line up on a calendar-2026 basis?
grading: Reference-free recency: use each company’s latest guide before the run timestamp, date it and preserve its calendar/fiscal and lease definitions. At the October 1 snapshot, CY2026: Alphabet $195–205B; Meta $130–145B including finance-lease principal; Amazon ~$220B cash capex; Microsoft ~$175B including finance leases/excluding operating leases. Do not treat Microsoft’s fiscal FY2027 or Q1 figures as calendar totals, or invent a harmonized cash basis.
answer: As of October 1, 2026, all four provide calendar-2026 capex numbers: Alphabet USD 195–205 billion (July 22 Q2 call); [G28-E1] Meta USD 130–145 billion including finance-lease principal payments (July 29 Q2 release); [G28-E2] Amazon approximately USD 220 billion in cash capex (July 30 Q2 call); [G28-E3] Microsoft approximately USD 175 billion (July 29 FY2026 Q4 call), including finance leases but excluding operating leases. Microsoft lowered the displayed capex amount because extending building useful lives shifts some future leases to operating classification; investment expectations apart from that change were unchanged. [G28-E4] Nominal ordering is Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, but the lease definitions differ, so these are not fully harmonized cash-spending measures. Microsoft separately expects FY2027 capex to grow YoY and Q1 FY2027 capex above USD 50 billion; those fiscal guides are not additional CY2026 totals. [G28-E4]

output.answer:
Here is the current capital expenditure guidance for each company on a **calendar-2026** basis, based on their most recent earnings reports and guidance updates:

| Company | Calendar 2026 CapEx Guidance | Year-over-Year Trend (vs. 2025) |
|---------|-----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Alphabet** | **$195 – $205 billion** | Up from ~$91–92B in 2025 |
| **Amazon** | **~$220 billion** | Up from ~$132B in 2025 |
| **Microsoft** | **~$175 billion** | Up ~61% from calendar 2025 |
| **Meta** | **$130 – $145 billion** | Up from ~$72B in 2025 |

### How They Line Up on a Calendar-2026 Basis

**Combined spending for these four companies is now approaching ~$725 billion** for the calendar year, up from roughly $400–$420 billion in 2025—a nearly 80% increase in aggregate.

- **Amazon** is the largest single spender at roughly **$220B**, primarily driven by AWS AI infrastructure. It recently raised its outlook from an initial ~$200B. Source: [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/amazon-raised-2026-capex-guide-114017457.html)

- **Alphabet** has steadily ratcheted up guidance multiple times this year, from an initial **$175–185B** range to the most recent **$195–205B**. CFO Anat Ashkenazi has cited the need to relieve compute capacity constraints across Search, Cloud, and Gemini. Source: [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/alphabet-stock-sinks-after-google-parent-announces-180-billion-spending-plan-for-2026-in-massive-ai-bet-155410864.html)

- **Microsoft** had initially guided to roughly **$190 billion** for calendar 2026, but CFO Amy Hood recently lowered the *reported* figure to **~$175 billion** due to an accounting change (extending data-center useful lives from 15 to 25 years), which shifts some leases from finance to operating treatment. Actual dollars being deployed on infrastructure remain very similar; the FY2026 exit run rate remains robust. Source: [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/microsoft-holds-line-ai-spending-154737639.html)

- **Meta** has also raised guidance three times over the past year, stepping from **$115–135B** to **$125–145B** to the current **$130–145B** range, focused on AI training and inference clusters as well as Reality Labs infrastructure. Source: [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/mark-zuckerbergs-meta-saw-free-101100387.html)

### Why the Figures Keep Climbing
All four companies cite the same dynamic: AI demand is outstripping installed compute capacity, forcing an infrastructure "arms race." Supply-chain inflation—particularly in memory, networking and power/connectivity components—is adding to the total bill, with Microsoft noting ~$25B of its 2026 budget is simply higher component pricing versus prior plans.
